Aciotis acuminifolia.presentation: Its upright, angular stems bear opposite leaves crossed by parallel veins. Their colour ranges from green to red, with a reddish underside; young leaves sometimes have slightly raised edges. This plant from tropical South America brings a neat outline to the midground.
Aciotis acuminifolia.culture: Provide soft water and a steady supply of nutrients. Strong lighting deepens the red tones; CO₂ supports its submerged growth. It can also grow above the surface and be grown emersed, as long as the air stays very humid.

Alternanthera aquatica.origine: Tropical South America, southern South America
Alternanthera aquatica.presentation: This South American plant grows long floating shoots whose swollen internodes hold air. In marshes and on banks, its roots anchor in the mud and its stems rise above the water. Its sprawling habit sets it apart from the small Alternanthera usually planted in groups.
Alternanthera aquatica.culture: Allow plenty of room: in the wild its shoots can reach several metres. It suits a spacious setup that lets it grow at the surface better than a small submerged group. In nature it anchors in nutrient-rich muddy bottoms; avoid presenting it as just another red foreground plant.

Amblystegium serpens.origine: North Africa, Europe, Asia, Australia, New Zealand, the Americas
Amblystegium serpens.presentation: A moss with tiny leaves whose look changes between open air and aquarium. On land it forms branching mats; underwater its shoots grow finer and stand up. This delicate habit earned it the trade name “nano moss”. It grows naturally on damp soil, wood and rocks.
Amblystegium serpens.culture: It can be grown submerged, although it is not naturally aquatic. Low to high light is given for this entry. It is propagated by dividing clumps or separating shoots. Bear in mind that the compact cushion seen out of water does not exactly predict its shape in the tank.

Ammannia crassicaulis.origine: West Africa, Central Africa, East Africa, Madagascar region
Ammannia crassicaulis.presentation: Native to the tropical wetlands of Africa and Madagascar, this plant is also known as Nesaea crassicaulis. Its tones range from yellowish green to pale red. It looks very much like Ammannia gracilis, usually redder, and the two are often confused in the trade.
Ammannia crassicaulis.culture: It needs strong lighting and rather soft water, in a tank suited to demanding plants. Cuttings are used to fill out a group of stems. Check the identity of a plant bought as Nesaea: the source notes that many plants sold under that name are actually Ammannia gracilis.

Anubias barteri var. nana.origine: Cameroon: shallow water in fast-flowing forest rivers (Central Africa)
Anubias barteri var. nana.presentation:
A dwarf variety of *Anubias barteri*, an aroid from Central and West Africa. It comes from Cameroon, where it grows in shallow water in fast-flowing forest rivers, but its wild sites remain poorly known. The Danish nursery Tropica started growing it in 1970; it has become one of the most widespread aquarium plants in Europe, Asia and North America.

A creeping rhizome bears thick, dark green leaves that live for several years. It often flowers underwater, with the small inflorescence typical of aroids, and plant-eating fish leave it alone.
Anubias barteri var. nana.culture:
Almost indestructible, to the point of being nicknamed “the plastic plant that grows”: it is as happy under very low light as under strong lighting, with or without CO2. Its rhizome must never be buried or it rots: tie it to a root or a stone with fishing line until its roots take hold.

Because it grows slowly, algae have time to settle on its old leaves; under strong light it is best placed in a shady corner. It is propagated by cutting the rhizome into two or more pieces. It goes in the foreground of a large tank or the midground of a nano tank.

Aponogeton crispus.presentation: Long leaves with wavy edges give this plant from Sri Lanka a supple, voluminous outline. In nature it lives in seasonal pools, but in the aquarium it can keep growing without an enforced rest. It flowers readily and suits planting alone or in a group in the background.
Aponogeton crispus.culture: Set aside a fairly large tank: the leaves can reach the surface and shade their neighbours. A nutrient-rich substrate and enough light help it grow; added CO₂ is not essential. Remove damaged leaves at their base. It is propagated by division or by seed.

Bacopa australis.origine: Tropical South America, southern South America
Bacopa australis.presentation: Its small, soft, bright green leaves form lighter bushes than those of Bacopa caroliniana. Young leaves can turn red under intense lighting. Native to southern Brazil and Argentina, it adds volume in the foreground or midground and can fill the background of a small aquarium.
Bacopa australis.culture: Under medium light the stems mostly grow upwards; with more light they may spread out. CO₂ and balanced fertilisation improve growth without being essential. Trim the groups before they become too dense, or their base will lack light. Replant the cut tips to propagate the plant.

Bacopa caroliniana.presentation: This Bacopa from the marshes of the southeastern United States bears fairly thick oval leaves arranged around straight stems. When crushed they give off a lemony scent. Their green can turn bronze under intense lighting. Planted in a group, it makes an even stand that contrasts with fine foliage.
Bacopa caroliniana.culture: Give good light and plant the stems in a group, possibly stepped so the stand reads clearly. Suitable fertilisation supports growth; CO₂ remains a bonus. The tips and side shoots are easy to replant. Out of water it takes on a creeping habit and can produce purple flowers.

Bacopa crenata.origine: West Africa, Central Africa, East Africa, Madagascar region
Bacopa crenata.presentation: This Bacopa from the wetlands of Africa and Madagascar grows supple stems, sometimes creeping at the base, that can root at the nodes. Its oval to lance-shaped leaves have a scalloped edge. In the wild, small white, sometimes slightly purple flowers appear in the leaf axils.
Bacopa crenata.culture: In the aquarium this entry needs strong light and is rated difficult. Cuttings let you renew the group. The botanical sources describe its natural marshes and ditches but give no complete method for growing it submerged: watch how it takes rather than expecting the toughness of the more common Bacopa.

Bacopa lanigera.presentation: This Brazilian Bacopa looks like Bacopa caroliniana, but its emersed stem is covered with hairs, hence its name meaning woolly. Its interest goes beyond the foliage: the difference between its land and water forms is worth watching when buying and acclimatising it.
Bacopa lanigera.culture: Provide strong light if you try it in the aquarium. Its long-term growth underwater calls for caution, though: the source reports conflicting information on whether it can be grown submerged. Do not choose it assuming it will behave exactly like Bacopa caroliniana; watch the condition of new shoots.

Baldellia ranunculoides.presentation: This plant of European wetlands forms a rosette. In the open air it bears lance-shaped leaves and small pale flowers; underwater the foliage becomes narrow and linear. The group includes several closely related forms, some of which produce runners while others stay as rosettes.
Baldellia ranunculoides.culture: It is mainly of interest for a cool-water aquarium. Temperatures above 20 °C are mentioned, but there are few reports of growing it underwater. Watch the exact form of your plant and how it spreads: the differences between subspecies affect its growth and mean a carpet of runners cannot be promised every time.

Barclaya longifolia.presentation: Although related to water lilies, Barclaya longifolia produces no floating leaves. Its long, wavy leaves may be green or reddish; the green form keeps a red underside. A young rosette recalls a Cryptocoryne, then gradually takes up the space of a large solitary plant.
Barclaya longifolia.culture: Give it warm water and enough light. Feeding the roots can boost its size; a small pot helps contain its growth. Its tender leaves are easily damaged. It may lose all its foliage during a rest period and then sprout again: do not throw the rhizome away as soon as the leaves disappear.

Blyxa aubertii.origine: East Africa, Madagascar region, South Asia, Southeast Asia, East Asia, Australia
Blyxa aubertii.presentation: Blyxa aubertii is a true aquatic plant, found both in rice fields and in running water. Its natural range stretches from southern Asia to Australia, with populations in Africa and Madagascar. It forms a rosette, offering an alternative to groups of stem plants.
Blyxa aubertii.culture: Provide medium to strong light and soft to moderately hard water. Propagation by seed is among the methods given for this entry. It remains uncommon in the hobby: check the plant's name, as Blyxa echinosperma was treated as a variety of this species in the source consulted.

Bolbitis heteroclita \"difformis\".presentation: This small fern from the Philippines is sold under names such as “mini Bolbitis” or “Davallia”, although it is not a Davallia. Its divided leaves recall parsley when it grows out of water. Submerged, it stays smaller and grows thicker leaves, with extremely slow growth.
Bolbitis heteroclita \"difformis\".culture: It does best in a humid terrarium or a warm paludarium. Growing it underwater is possible, but expect it to settle in very slowly. It can be tied to a lava stone with thread. Check its identity when buying: “mini Bolbitis” also refers to other small ferns whose aquarium performance is uncertain.

Bolbitis heudelotii.origine: West Africa, Central Africa, East Africa, southern Africa
Bolbitis heudelotii.presentation: This African fern bears divided leaves, dark green and translucent underwater. Its creeping rhizome clings to stones and wood in tropical streams. Paired with a root and mosses, it makes a midground stand reminiscent of river vegetation.
Bolbitis heudelotii.culture: Tie the rhizome to the decor without burying it. Soft, slightly acidic water, a little current and CO₂ help it develop. Growth remains slow and the brittle foliage needs gentle handling. To propagate it, divide the rhizome into pieces each carrying several leaves.

Cabomba aquatica.presentation: Its submerged leaves split into a multitude of fine segments, like wide fans. This South American Cabomba comes in several colours; the green form is the most common in the trade. When the shoots reach the surface, they can bear round floating leaves and yellow flowers.
Cabomba aquatica.culture: Plant the stems in the background with enough light to keep the stand vigorous. It is rated difficult and needs regular attention to the state of the shoots. Cuttings let you renew the group. Allow for height and space: the leaves can be much wider than those of other Cabomba.

Cabomba caroliniana var. caroliniana.presentation: The finely divided leaves of green cabomba bring lightness to the background. In good conditions its stems quickly reach the surface, where floating leaves and white flowers may appear. It comes from lakes, ponds and rivers of the Americas.
Cabomba caroliniana var. caroliniana.culture: Lighting plays a major role: too little light or too much heat weakens the stems. CO₂ boosts growth without always being needed. Replant the tips after trimming; the cut bases can take a while to produce side shoots. Keep its growth in check so it does not take over the stand.

Cabomba furcata.presentation: This very fine-leaved Cabomba brings red and pink tones to the middle or back of the tank. It comes from slow waters of Central and South America. Its colour is appealing, but it needs more careful conditions than common stem plants.
Cabomba furcata.culture: Strong lighting, CO₂ and a steady supply of nutrients are essential for good growth. Deficiencies can slow the shoots, lengthen the internodes and darken the leaves. A nutrient-rich substrate can help. Propagate by tip cuttings and trim regularly once the stand is established; it cannot be grown emersed.

Calliergonella cuspidata.origine: North Africa, Madagascar region, Europe, North Asia, West Asia, Central Asia, South Asia, East Asia, North America, Caribbean
Calliergonella cuspidata.presentation: This moss of damp meadows and ditches forms light green cushions, with fairly stiff, pointed shoot tips. Underwater it grows more upright and branches less than in open air. Intense lighting encourages branching and a bushier look.
Calliergonella cuspidata.culture: The experiences cited show it can be grown submerged and grows fairly fast. It can be used as an upright moss, while staying stiffer and paler than Drepanocladus aduncus. Propagate by dividing clumps. Its outline depends on the light: give the shoots room rather than expecting a permanently flat carpet.

Callitriche palustris agg..presentation: The water starworts of this group bear soft leaves on thin stems. Submerged, they mostly grow narrow leaves; at the surface, the tips form rosettes of broader leaves. The suffix “agg.” refers to a set of closely related species, not a precise botanical identification of the plant.
Callitriche palustris agg..culture: Some plants of the group seem able to last in the aquarium, even above 20 °C, but experience remains limited. Cuttings are used to renew the stems. Watch the form you receive and how its foliage changes: starworts sold for ponds are not necessarily all the same species, and identifying them often needs the flowers or fruit.

Cardamine lyrata.presentation: Its supple stems bear small, light green, kidney-shaped leaves. This plant of East Asian wetlands climbs among its neighbours and can run over the roots of the decor. In cool water the leaves are larger; warmer water produces much smaller foliage.
Cardamine lyrata.culture: It suits cool tanks or moderately heated tropical ones. Good light prevents overly thin stems; CO₂ boosts growth without being essential. To keep a bush in the midground, trim often. Stem pieces and side shoots root quickly when replanted.

Ceratophyllum demersum.origine: Almost worldwide: still or slow waters of Europe, Africa, Asia and the Americas
Ceratophyllum demersum.presentation:
A rootless plant, extremely well adapted to life underwater: its inconspicuous flowers open submerged, and the pollen drifts through the water to the female flowers. The name actually covers several closely related species, told apart only by the number of spines on their fruit, which do not form in the aquarium.

In temperate regions it spends the winter as short, compact shoots that sink to the bottom, then grows again in spring: it therefore also suits garden ponds.
Ceratophyllum demersum.culture:
Very easy and very fast-growing, in soft as well as very hard water and over a wide range of temperatures. CO2 is not needed. It absorbs nutrients very quickly, which makes it an ally against algae.

Let it float under the surface, or keep it on the bottom by pushing the base of the stems into the substrate or weighting them. It propagates simply by fragmentation of the stems and must be trimmed often. Its clumps give shrimp hiding places and surfaces to graze, and fish a place to spawn.

Ceratophyllum submersum.origine: Africa, Europe, West Asia, Southeast Asia, East Asia, North America
Ceratophyllum submersum.presentation: Softer and finer than Ceratophyllum demersum, this hornwort bears leaves split into many threads. The stems stay light green, while the foliage can turn orange under intense light. Rootless, it quickly forms a floating cover that can shelter fry.
Ceratophyllum submersum.culture: Let it float under the surface or hold the tips in the substrate. Medium light is enough; CO₂ is not essential but speeds up growth. Trim often so the vegetation does not take over the whole tank. Its delicate foliage makes it a lighter alternative to the usual hornwort.

Ceratopteris cornuta.origine: West Africa, Central Africa, East Africa, Madagascar region, West Asia, South Asia, Southeast Asia, Australia
Ceratopteris cornuta.presentation: In the trade this aquatic fern is recognised by its broadly lobed leaves, less finely cut than those sold as Ceratopteris thalictroides. The forms are nonetheless close and hard to tell apart botanically. It brings broad foliage to the tank rather than a network of small leaves on stems.
Ceratopteris cornuta.culture: It can be grown floating or planted in the substrate. Provide medium to strong light and room for fast growth. The young plantlets that form on it are used to propagate it. The trade name alone does not guarantee a precise identification: some related ferns are hard to tell apart without examining their spores.

Ceratopteris pteridoides.origine: South Asia, Southeast Asia, East Asia, North America, Central America, Caribbean, tropical South America
Ceratopteris pteridoides.presentation: This surface fern has thick, spongy leaf stalks that keep the leaves afloat. The young leaves are entire, then the adults develop broad lobes with a triangular outline. Many plantlets may appear in the notches of older leaves.
Ceratopteris pteridoides.culture: Grow it at the surface or as a marsh plant on damp soil; it does not last fully submerged. Leave room for the foliage. The plantlets formed on old leaves are used to propagate it. Emersed growing with plenty of light and a rich soil favours the fertile fronds.

Ceratopteris thalictroides.origine: South Asia, Southeast Asia, East Asia, Australia, Oceania, North America, Central America, Caribbean, tropical South America
Ceratopteris thalictroides.presentation: Its light green, deeply cut foliage quickly forms a large, airy bush. This amphibious fern lives in shallow water and muddy tropical soils. Floating, it gives fry cover and some fish a support for their bubble nests.
Ceratopteris thalictroides.culture: It grows floating or rooted in the substrate, where it can become especially bulky. Medium light is already enough to grow it; more light, nutrients and CO₂ speed up its development. Plan a large tank for a single plant. The plantlets formed on the leaves let you renew the plants.

Clinopodium brownei.presentation: Rounded leaves with scalloped edges line its green, angular stems. When crushed they smell of mint. This American plant has sometimes been sold as Lindernia anagallis. Underwater it grows mostly upright, with rather few side branches.
Clinopodium brownei.culture: Place the stems in the midground or background depending on the height you want. Good light supports its growth and cuttings let you thicken the group. Its emersed form is more creeping: a plant received from land culture may therefore look different from how it will grow in the aquarium.

Crassula helmsii.presentation: This aquatic Crassula from Australia and New Zealand stands out among the many terrestrial succulents of its genus. It colonises very varied habitats and copes with calm water as well as strong currents. Introduced elsewhere, it can form highly invasive stands.
Crassula helmsii.culture: It tolerates a wide range of conditions, with medium to strong light given for aquarium growing. Cuttings are used to renew the stand. Follow the spread of the stems and remove the excess to keep space for the other plants; its vigour must not be mistaken for modest growth.

Crinum calamistratum.presentation: Very long, narrow, dark green and strongly wavy leaves give this African Crinum a supple and unusual outline. It forms a smaller bulb than other Crinum, but its foliage can take up much of the decor. A single plant shows off its crinkled ribbons particularly well.
Crinum calamistratum.culture: It grows slowly and needs less light than other Crinum. Well-established plants can produce small bulbs used for propagation. Allow room for the long leaves rather than judging its size from the bulb alone. Tropica also notes that plant-eating fish do not eat its foliage.

Crinum natans.presentation: This Crinum from tropical Africa grows naturally in the mud at the bottom of permanent streams. Its pleated leaves can stay submerged or float, while large, fragrant white flowers rise above the water. Its bulbous habit gives the decor a different outline from a stem plant.
Crinum natans.culture: Provide medium to strong light and give the plant time to settle: it grows slowly. Young offshoots can be separated to propagate it. Give it a place in the middle or back of the tank, where you can follow the foliage rising towards the surface without crowding its neighbours.

Crinum thaianum.presentation: This large bulbous plant grows long, smooth, ribbon-like leaves. Its root system becomes extensive in the substrate, while the foliage gradually takes up a lot of volume. It suits a spot where its outline can stay visible without being squeezed between groups of plants.
Crinum thaianum.culture: Allow room in the substrate and around the plant. It is propagated by separating the young bulbs that appear at the base of the main bulb. Before replanting these young plants, the source recommends shortening their long roots. Its slow growth calls for patience rather than frequent moves.

Cryptocoryne wendtii.presentation:
An aroid from Sri Lanka, described in 1958 by the Dutch botanist Hendrik de Wit, who named it after the aquarist and author Albert Wendt. It is one of the hardiest and best-selling cryptocorynes.

It forms a rosette of lance-shaped leaves with wavy edges. The species is very variable and its cultivated forms differ mainly in colour: green (“Green”), brown or bronze (“Tropica”), or “Mi Oya”, named after the river in Sri Lanka where it was found.
Cryptocoryne wendtii.culture:
Easy, it makes do with low light and, like most Sri Lankan cryptocorynes, grows well in hard water. It is planted in groups in the foreground or midground; on its own, with no neighbours, it spreads its leaves almost flat on the ground.

Cryptocorynes cope badly with sudden changes (transplanting, moving from emersed nursery growing to the aquarium): the plant sometimes loses all its leaves, which “melt”, then regrows from the rhizome within about a month. It is best placed in an aquarium that has been running for a few months. It spreads by runners.

Cuphea anagalloidea.presentation: Formerly circulated as Rotala sp. “Araguaia”, this small stem plant comes from Brazil. Underwater, the upper side of the leaves turns a strong red, sometimes flecked with green; out of water the foliage stays green and the plant grows taller. It makes a fairly delicate colour accent.
Cuphea anagalloidea.culture: Provide strong light to bring out the colour and soft water suited to a demanding plant. It is propagated by tip cuttings or side shoots. Detailed growing reports remain limited: watch how it takes and adjust feeding rather than expecting it to behave like a Rotala just because it once bore that name.

Didiplis diandra.presentation: Its narrow leaves give stands a fine texture, unlike large-leaved plants. Native to the eastern United States, it turns from green to orange or red tones when conditions suit it. It adds an accent of colour and structure to the midground or background.
Didiplis diandra.culture: Insufficient lighting can make the base of the stems die back. Under strong light, keep up a regular supply of nutrients, especially iron and trace elements. CO₂ improves vigour without always being essential. Cutting the tips encourages branching; replant the cuttings to fill out or rejuvenate the stand.

Drepanocladus aduncus.origine: North Africa, Central Africa, East Africa, Europe, North Asia, West Asia, Central Asia, East Asia, New Zealand, North America, Central America
Drepanocladus aduncus.presentation: This aquatic moss forms dark green tufts whose shoots and leaves can curve like a sickle. In low light the submerged stems stand up and branch little; near the surface they become bushier. It recalls the mosses sold as “Stringy Moss”.
Drepanocladus aduncus.culture: It suits cool tanks as well as warmer, simply equipped aquariums. Tie it to wood or stone, then keep its growth in check if conditions let it run wild. Propagate by division. Check its identity: the source notes that some mosses sold as “Aduncus Moss” belong to other species.

Echinodorus grisebachii 'Bleherae'.origine: Tropical South America, probably the Amazon; the *E. grisebachii* group is widespread in tropical America
Echinodorus grisebachii 'Bleherae'.presentation:
Known to aquarists as *Echinodorus bleheri*, it is probably the most widespread sword plant in aquariums. Its exact origin remains unclear, perhaps the Amazon; it belongs to the *Echinodorus grisebachii* group, like the “Amazonicus” and “Parviflorus” forms. It was long sold as *E. paniculatus*, a name that actually refers to quite a different plant. GBIF now places the species in the genus *Aquarius*.

In the wild these plants spend most of the year underwater and only form aerial leaves and flower stalks when the water recedes. The most common form is triploid: its small flowers, 1.5 cm at most, are sterile.
Echinodorus grisebachii 'Bleherae'.culture:
Easy and vigorous, it adapts to very varied water and grows even in a dimly lit aquarium, because its leaves climb towards the light. Its size is often underestimated: the height given is that of the first months, but a healthy adult plant exceeds 60 cm in both height and width. It is therefore for large aquariums, where it makes a superb specimen plant; for a medium tank, the “Parviflorus” form stays around 30 cm.

A nutrient-rich substrate helps it grow, and the large leaves that rob the plants below of light must be cut. It is propagated with the plantlets that form on the flower stalk, or by dividing the rhizome.

Egeria densa.presentation: Its closely set leaves, arranged in whorls, give the stems a dense look. This South American plant has long been widespread in the hobby and can grow rooted or floating. Its vigorous growth uses up the available nutrients and quickly builds a planted background.
Egeria densa.culture: It prefers fairly cool, mineral-rich water, while tolerating more heat for a while. Keep space between the stems and renew the group with cuttings when it grows too tall. To the naked eye the leaves look almost smooth, unlike those of Egeria najas, which are more visibly toothed: check the plant before comparing their needs.

Egeria najas.origine: Tropical South America, southern South America
Egeria najas.presentation: Its narrow, clearly toothed leaves surround the stems in tight groups. This South American plant looks like Egeria densa, but has finer foliage and copes better with heat. It remains an undemanding option for a background stand in a tropical tank.
Egeria najas.culture: It is easily propagated by cuttings and needs little special equipment. Medium to strong light supports its growth. Trim and replant the shoots to keep a balanced group. When buying, look at the teeth on the leaves: Egeria densa and Hydrilla verticillata can be confused with this species.

Eichhornia azurea.origine: Tropical and subtropical America, from Mexico to Argentina, and the West Indies
Eichhornia azurea.presentation: Underwater, its long, narrow leaves line up on each side of the stem, giving the shoot the look of a palm frond. This American plant looks very different at the surface, with spoon-shaped aerial leaves. Its outline is best shown off as a specimen plant in a large tank.
Eichhornia azurea.culture: Provide a tall aquarium and space around the shoots; the submerged leaves are fragile and do not like being crushed during planting. Take cuttings of the tops before they reach the surface if you want to keep the aquatic form. A top that has already grown aerial leaves may keep producing that form after replanting.

Eichhornia crassipes.presentation: The water hyacinth forms floating rosettes with swollen leaf stalks that act as floats. Long, dark roots hang beneath the leaves, while mauve flowers may appear above the water. It multiplies quickly by runners and soon covers a large area.
Eichhornia crassipes.culture: It needs an open, spacious setup, strong light and nutrient-rich water. Growth can slow in the cold or when the plant lacks food. Thin out the rosettes to let light through below the surface. It does not survive frost and can become invasive when introduced outside its natural range.

Eichhornia diversifolia.origine: Central America, Caribbean, tropical South America
Eichhornia diversifolia.presentation: This stem plant grows dense foliage whose outline can recall a small palm. If it reaches the surface, it produces oval floating leaves and may bloom in blue. Its deep green makes a focal point in the middle or back of a planted aquarium.
Eichhornia diversifolia.culture: Avoid shaded areas: the leaves can turn transparent and then drop. Added CO₂ and a steady supply of nutrients encourage sturdy stems; deficiencies in particular make the bottom of the stand die back. Leave room for branching, then replant the side shoots to propagate the plant.

Elatine hydropiper.presentation: Its tiny leaves make a fresh green lawn, finer than Glossostigma elatinoides and usually slower to take over the tank. It is valued for the foreground of small aquariums but can also form a large sheet in a spacious tank. Wild populations live in European and Asian aquatic habitats.
Elatine hydropiper.culture: It is demanding and needs strong light, without the carpet being hidden under taller plants. Propagation by fragments lets you fill thin patches. The identity of aquarium strains has been debated in the source: related Elatine can look alike, and a sure identification sometimes needs flowers and fruit.

Elatine triandra.origine: Europe, Central Asia, South Asia, Southeast Asia, East Asia, Australia, New Zealand
Elatine triandra.presentation: This small creeping plant naturally colonises bare ground in ponds, shallow streams and rice fields that dry out from time to time. Its range is very wide, from temperate regions to the tropics. Its low habit suits foreground planting rather than a background stand.
Elatine triandra.culture: Provide medium to strong light for this carpeting plant. Fragments let you multiply the planting and fill gaps. Plants in the trade may come from Asia, but their exact origin is uncertain. Do not mistake the conditions of its seasonal habitat for a need to let the carpet dry out in the aquarium.

Eleocharis acicularis.origine: Almost worldwide: pond edges and shallow water in Europe, Asia, North Africa, the Americas and Australia
Eleocharis acicularis.presentation:
A small sedge with hair-thin leaves, called “dwarf hairgrass” in English. It grows on pond edges and in shallow water almost everywhere in the world, central Europe included, and is also sold as a pond plant.

Underwater it forms tufts of upright, mid-green leaves 10 to 20 cm long. *Eleocharis pusilla*, often sold as “E. parvula”, looks like it but stays lower (5 cm), paler and has curved leaves.
Eleocharis acicularis.culture:
It thrives in almost any aquarium, as long as it has room and light, with no plants shading it. After planting, its runners spread over the substrate and form a dense lawn 6 to 15 cm high according to Tropica. It prefers soft to moderately hard water that is not too warm.

If the carpet grows too tall, trim it carefully with scissors. To propagate it, separate tufts and replant them further along.

Eleocharis pusilla (\"E. parvula\").presentation: Thin, light green stems, often leaning to the sides, form a low lawn. The plant sold in the hobby as Eleocharis parvula is often attributed to E. pusilla, native to Australia and New Zealand. It usually stays shorter than Eleocharis acicularis, which makes it interesting for the foreground.
Eleocharis pusilla (\"E. parvula\").culture: Medium to strong light supports its carpeting growth. It spreads by runners: leave space between the tufts for them to extend. The trade name “parvula” does not guarantee the species, as several related Eleocharis circulate under that label. A form that arrives taller is therefore not necessarily the same plant.

Elodea canadensis.presentation: Canadian waterweed is one of the most famous aquatic plants of the past, even though today it is found more in ponds than in aquariums. Native to North America, it long formed huge stands after being introduced into Europe. It looks very much like Elodea nuttallii.
Elodea canadensis.culture: This entry favours cool setups; its published optimal range lies below that of many tropical plants. Cuttings let you renew the stems. Check the name of the plant you buy: pond waterweeds are often sold with a rough identification, and Elodea nuttallii copes better with high temperatures.

Elodea nuttallii.presentation: This North American waterweed has longer leaves, sometimes slightly twisted, than Elodea canadensis. It grows in varied waters, including very nutrient-rich ones, and can form large masses. It is often sold as a pond plant under the name of its close relative.
Elodea nuttallii.culture: It copes better than Elodea canadensis with temperatures above 20 °C, without becoming a plant for very warm tanks only. Trimming and cuttings keep the group of stems under control. Watch how much space it takes, as it can spread a lot, and check its identity when buying.

Eriocaulon cinereum.origine: Africa, South Asia, Southeast Asia, East Asia, Australia
Eriocaulon cinereum.presentation: This small rosette recalls a green sea urchin, with narrow leaves radiating from the centre. It adds a graphic accent to the foreground. Despite its modest size, its root system can be several times longer than its leaves: most of the plant is hidden in the substrate.
Eriocaulon cinereum.culture: Provide a nutrient-rich substrate, strong light and CO₂, plus balanced fertilisation in the water. Growth remains slow even in good conditions. To separate an offshoot, free the plant and cleanly cut the link with the mother plant. Do not pull the two rosettes apart without freeing their roots.

Eriocaulon setaceum.origine: Africa, South Asia, Southeast Asia, East Asia, Australia, tropical South America
Eriocaulon setaceum.presentation: Its fine, almost needle-like leaves give the shoots a light, delicate texture. Unlike a small-rosette Eriocaulon, this species grows taller and can branch a lot. It suits as a fine accent in the middle or back of a tank designed for demanding plants.
Eriocaulon setaceum.culture: It needs very soft water, an acidic substrate, strong light and CO₂. Keep up a regular supply of nutrients. It tolerates trimming poorly: only step in when necessary and prefer renewing the plant with short cuttings rather than repeatedly cutting back an old stand. Long cuttings readily grow unsightly roots on the stems.

Fissidens fontanus.origine: Europe, North and Central America; more rarely reported in South America, southern Africa and Oceania
Fissidens fontanus.presentation: Known in the trade as “Phoenix moss”, this truly aquatic moss bears leaves in two rows, giving each shoot the look of a small feather. Dark green and supple, it forms tufts attached to wood or stone. It grows naturally in rivers and lakes, sometimes deep in the shade.
Fissidens fontanus.culture: It can live with little light and attaches to the decor with its rhizoids. Propagate it by separating the tufts. Handle the shoots gently and keep them damp while you work: this moss dries out quickly in the air and becomes brittle. The Asian origin of a commercial batch does not necessarily match its natural range.

Fontinalis antipyretica.presentation: Willow moss is a true aquatic moss, widespread in running and still waters of the northern hemisphere. Its look varies a great deal with conditions and cultivated forms. It brings river vegetation to the decor rather than the foliage of a classic stem plant.
Fontinalis antipyretica.culture: It is grown fully submerged, with low to strong light depending on the tank. Dividing clumps is used to multiply the planting. Check the identification: local Leptodictyum-type mosses are often taken for Fontinalis, and the different forms of the species do not all keep the same size.

Fontinalis hypnoides.origine: Europe, Central Asia, East Asia, North America
Fontinalis hypnoides.presentation: Finer and softer than Fontinalis antipyretica, this moss has small, narrow leaves that are not folded lengthwise. Its much-branched shoots gradually form dark green bushes. It lives only underwater, mostly in calm or slow-flowing habitats.
Fontinalis hypnoides.culture: Keep it submerged rather than growing it in air. Medium to strong light is given for this entry. Divide the clumps to multiply the planting and leave room for the branches. Its delicate texture is interesting when you want a lighter stand than that of the usual willow moss.

Glossostigma elatinoides.presentation: Its small spoon-shaped leaves sit on creeping runners that can cover the ground quickly. This plant from Australia and New Zealand has become a classic of aquascape foregrounds. Well lit, it makes a low carpet; in the shade it stands up and loses that look.
Glossostigma elatinoides.culture: Provide strong light, CO₂ and regular fertilisation. When planting, spread small groups to give the runners room to colonise the ground. Yellowing leaves or slower growth can signal nutrient shortages. A plant sold in emersed form must first produce new underwater foliage before giving an even carpet.

Gymnocoronis spilanthoides.origine: Tropical South America, southern South America
Gymnocoronis spilanthoides.presentation: This South American plant can grow upright stems or floating mats, with opposite leaves with wavy edges. Hollow internodes help it float. When emersed it produces clusters of small, very fragrant white or pinkish flowers. Its size and habit can change greatly with the water level.
Gymnocoronis spilanthoides.culture: Allow room for fast growth. Stem fragments can root at the nodes: cuttings are therefore easy to multiply, but detached pieces can also settle elsewhere. Submerged growing does not necessarily give the large bush seen on a bank. Keep the shoots in check and keep track of where the plant came from.

Hedyotis salzmannii.origine: Tropical South America, southern South America
Hedyotis salzmannii.presentation: Underwater, this South American plant bears light green, narrow oval leaves along thin upright stems. Out of water it becomes more creeping and may produce small white or pinkish flowers. It has circulated under the names Oldenlandia salzmannii and Bacopa sp. “Pantanal”.
Hedyotis salzmannii.culture: Plant in a group and multiply the shoots by cuttings. Good light supports its growth. When buying, tell the real plant apart from a Bacopa monnieri sold under the same name: the latter has clearly thicker, fleshier leaves and stems. The trade name alone is therefore not enough to recognise this entry.

Helanthium bolivianum.origine: Tropical South America, southern South America
Helanthium bolivianum.presentation: These small rosette plants produce runners and can gradually spread their planting. They belong to the group once classed among the small Echinodorus. The name Helanthium bolivianum, however, covers several interpretations and trade forms, whose habit and foliage may differ.
Helanthium bolivianum.culture: Provide medium to strong light and leave the runners some free ground around the plants. The young rosettes let you multiply the planting. Look at the form you actually receive before choosing its final place: the name “bolivianum” alone does not guarantee a very low lawn or a precise height.

Helanthium bolivianum \"quadricostatus\".presentation: “Quadricostatus” is a trade name used for several forms of Helanthium bolivianum. Some stay very low and form a fast ground cover; others can exceed twenty centimetres. The names Echinodorus magdalenensis or E. xinguensis are also found for these plants, which keeps the confusion going.
Helanthium bolivianum \"quadricostatus\".culture: Give the runners room, then separate the young rosettes to extend or contain the planting. Medium to strong light supports its growth. Check the form on sale before choosing it for a nano tank: not every plant labelled “quadricostatus” produces a carpet of the same height.

Hemianthus glomeratus.presentation: Its small leaves and many shoots make a dense, light green bush. This plant from Florida was long sold as Hemianthus micranthemoides, whereas the real species of that name is a different plant. It can grow upwards or spread out depending on the light.
Hemianthus glomeratus.culture: Good light gives a more compact stand; in the shade the stems stretch and the internodes spread apart. CO₂ speeds up growth and encourages branching. Keep up a regular supply of nutrients, then trim and replant the cuttings to keep the shape you want rather than letting the bush grow too tall.

Heteranthera dubia.presentation: This plant looks like a set of long, light green grass blades. It is larger and less demanding than its relative Heteranthera zosterifolia. Floating shoots may bear yellow star-shaped flowers, whereas its relative flowers in blue. It makes a light, unfussy planted background.
Heteranthera dubia.culture: Plant it in a group and replant the tops if the stems start floating at the surface. It suits cool tanks and tolerates various water qualities, with a preference for slightly mineral water. CO₂ is not essential. Its fast growth calls for regular trimming to keep space for neighbouring plants.

Heteranthera zosterifolia.origine: Tropical South America, southern South America
Heteranthera zosterifolia.presentation: Bright green lance-shaped leaves line stems that quickly build a full stand. This Brazilian plant suits compositions meant to contrast with dark or red foliage. By adjusting the trimming, it can be kept at different heights in the tank.
Heteranthera zosterifolia.culture: Medium light is already enough to grow it; more light and CO₂ give more vigorous growth. Watch the nutrients: transparent leaves can signal a lack of nitrogen, while a darker green can come with a lack of phosphorus. Cuttings let you renew the stand after trimming.

Hottonia palustris.presentation: Its divided leaves give this European plant a feathery look. In the wild the clumps stay submerged while the flower stalks rise above the water in spring. Despite resemblances to Limnophila or Myriophyllum, the leaves are not arranged in whorls. It is of interest for a cool-water tank layout.
Hottonia palustris.culture: Avoid shade and keep up a regular supply of nutrients, as the base of the shoots can die back when light is lacking. CO₂ encourages vigorous foliage. It prefers cool temperatures and the source advises against staying above 26 °C for long. Side shoots and cuttings let you rejuvenate the group.

Hydrilla verticillata.origine: East Africa, Europe, Central Asia, South Asia, Southeast Asia, East Asia, Australia
Hydrilla verticillata.presentation: The toothed leaves, arranged in whorls around the stems, recall those of waterweeds. This very variable plant can grow long upright shoots, creeping stems and resting buds in the soil. It is widespread and can form invasive stands when it finds favourable conditions.
Hydrilla verticillata.culture: Allow room and keep the length of the stems in check by trimming. Cuttings are used to renew the planting. To identify it, look at the visible teeth on the leaves and the spacing between their whorls: Hydrilla can be confused with Egeria. Its ability to regrow from resting organs makes its growth less predictable than a simple bunch of cuttings.

Hydrocotyle leucocephala.origine: Central America, Caribbean, tropical South America, southern South America
Hydrocotyle leucocephala.presentation: Its round, light green leaves sit on supple stems that can climb between other plants or run along the surface. This South American pennywort contrasts well with Anubias and dark foliage. It can be used in a stand, around a root or as a floating plant.
Hydrocotyle leucocephala.culture: Undemanding, it accepts a wide range of conditions and does not necessarily need CO₂. Good light and available nutrients nevertheless make it more vigorous. Side shoots are easy to take as cuttings. Yellowing leaf edges can signal a lack of iron; also keep in check the stems that begin to shade their neighbours.

Hydrocotyle sibthorpioides.origine: Africa, Madagascar region, South Asia, Southeast Asia, East Asia
Hydrocotyle sibthorpioides.presentation: This creeping pennywort bears small round leaves, much more modest than those of H. leucocephala. Its stems advance over the ground and can form a fine cover. It is also found under the trade name “Hydrocotyle maritima”, which can however refer to other plants.
Hydrocotyle sibthorpioides.culture: Underwater it needs strong light, CO₂ and a regular supply of nutrients. It does not suit a dark tank without growth support. Side shoots serve as cuttings. Emersed growing can quickly provide fragments to replant, but this land behaviour must not suggest that growing it underwater is as undemanding.

Hydrocotyle verticillata.origine: Africa, Australia, North America, Central America, Caribbean, tropical South America, southern South America
Hydrocotyle verticillata.presentation: Each leaf looks like a small parasol, with the stalk attached at the centre and no notch. The runners creep in or over the substrate and make a foreground dotted with these green discs. This pennywort from warm regions of the Americas thus differs from the climbing habit of H. leucocephala.
Hydrocotyle verticillata.culture: Light intensity affects its height: more light keeps it lower. CO₂ and balanced feeding help growth, but very generous feeding can enlarge the foliage. Trim the runners to contain the planting and keep gaps between the leaves rather than letting the whole foreground fill up.

Hygrophila balsamica.presentation: This Hygrophila from India and Sri Lanka can form a large, light green, much-branched stand. Trimming lets you either encourage a dense bush or keep more vertical stems. Its fast growth adds volume to the background but needs a lot of space and regular care.
Hygrophila balsamica.culture: Provide good light, CO₂ and available nutrients, especially iron. The source reports toxicity to animals for some old emersed strains, while noting that recent commercial strains differ on this point. Check the batch and how it was grown before adding it to a stocked tank. Take cuttings from the many side shoots.

Hygrophila corymbosa.presentation: This Asian Hygrophila produces long, broad, light green leaves. Its stems grow fast and branch out into a full stand. Undemanding, it is good for quickly building plant volume, provided you accept the trimming needed to keep the layout readable.
Hygrophila corymbosa.culture: Separate the stems of a bunch and remove the transport tie before planting. Space the plants, clear damaged leaves from their lower parts and let the roots develop. Trim often to keep the height in check; the cut parts are easy to replant and help fill out the stand.

Hygroryza aristata.presentation: This Asian grass floats thanks to swollen leaf sheaths. Its fairly broad, lance-shaped, water-repellent leaves make a surface cover very different from duckweed or a floating rosette. In open air, on damp soil, it also grows in a creeping way.
Hygroryza aristata.culture: Let it grow its shoots at the surface rather than trying to make it a fully submerged plant. Provide enough light and room for fast growth. Fragments let you renew the cover. Thin the planting if it becomes too dense, to keep light for the plants below.

Hymenasplenium obscurum.origine: East Africa, Madagascar region, South Asia, Southeast Asia, East Asia
Hymenasplenium obscurum.presentation: This fern circulated in the hobby under the wrong name Crepidomanes auriculatum. Its identification was clarified thanks to adult plants grown out of water. Also called Asplenium obscurum, it belongs to a different lineage from the small ferns sometimes sold under a similar name.
Hymenasplenium obscurum.culture: The profile lists it among epiphytes: attach it to the decor and expect very slow growth. Dividing the rhizome lets you propagate it. Detailed growing reports remain limited in the description consulted; check the plant's identity and watch how it takes before expecting it to behave like a Bolbitis or a true Crepidomanes.

Juncus repens.presentation: Its habit mixes that of a stem plant and a rosette: tufts of fine leaves appear at regular intervals along the shoots. Green under moderate light, this rush can take on reddish tones with more light and good feeding. It brings a grassy texture to the stand.
Juncus repens.culture: It accepts several light levels and its steady growth stays fairly easy to control. Replant a piece of stem cut below a tuft of leaves; it does not need to have roots already. Trimming lets you use it at the back, in the middle or even lower in the tank. Watch for spot algae on its long-lived leaves.

Lemna trisulca.origine: Africa, Europe, Asia, Australia, North America, Caribbean
Lemna trisulca.presentation: Unlike duckweeds sitting on the surface, this species forms cushions floating just below it. Its small fronds stay joined together in a branching network. It occurs naturally in calm waters and can hide under a cover of other duckweeds.
Lemna trisulca.culture: Let the fragments float in a calm area rather than planting them in the substrate. They make it easy to multiply the cushion. In the wild the winter form becomes shorter and can sink towards the bottom while continuing to grow slowly. Bear this in mind before writing off every submerged fragment as a lost plant.

Leptodictyum riparium.origine: North Africa, Europe, North Asia, West Asia, Central Asia, Southeast Asia, East Asia, Australia, Oceania, North America, Central America, Caribbean, tropical South America, southern South America
Leptodictyum riparium.presentation: This widespread aquatic moss forms shoots with flattened foliage that can grow fairly horizontal when the light allows. Its look depends a great deal on conditions. It is often called “Stringy Moss”, but the strictly upright moss sold under that name may belong to Drepanocladus aduncus.
Leptodictyum riparium.culture: It suits cool tanks as well as moderately warm tropical aquariums. Tie the tufts to wood or stone, then divide them to extend the planting. Do not promise an upright habit from the trade name alone: the same moss changes shape with the light, and several related species are confused in the trade.

Lilaeopsis brasiliensis.presentation: This South American plant forms a fine-leaved ground cover that recalls a small lawn. It can become very dense, but a truly compact turf depends on good lighting. Its runners link the young shoots and let the planting spread gradually across the foreground.
Lilaeopsis brasiliensis.culture: Plant small portions a few centimetres apart so they join up more easily. Choose an open spot, out of the shade of taller stands. Growth is slow: do not expect the carpet to close straight away. Tropica also mentions its use in ponds and its tolerance of low salinity, without making it a marine plant.

Lilaeopsis mauritiana.presentation: Native to Mauritius, this Lilaeopsis entered the trade as “Lilaeopsis sp. Mauritius” before its botanical description. It has the narrowest leaves of the Lilaeopsis species reported as grown in aquariums. Its very fine texture is interesting for low planting.
Lilaeopsis mauritiana.culture: Provide medium to strong light for this carpeting entry. It spreads by runners, which gradually extend the planting: leave free ground around the tufts. Detailed advice remains limited in the source description, so it is better to watch how fast it spreads than to promise the carpet will close within a set time.

Limnobium laevigatum.origine: Central America, Caribbean, tropical South America
Limnobium laevigatum.presentation: Its floating rosettes look like large duckweed and carry long roots that hang down into the tank. This Limnobium from Central and South America naturally lives in calm water. Its cover gives shifting shade and its roots can become part of the decor.
Limnobium laevigatum.culture: Set aside an area of calm surface. Runners quickly produce young rosettes; remove the surplus so as not to rob the bottom of light. Good feeding supports growth. With plenty of light and humidity, emersed leaves may appear. Replacing it with another frogbit does not guarantee the same temperature needs.

Limnobium spongia.presentation: This North American Limnobium has leaves that are more clearly heart-shaped and pointed than those of Limnobium laevigatum. It lives in calm or gently flowing water, but can also grow on mud as a marsh plant. It is grown less often today than its South American relative.
Limnobium spongia.culture: Let it take the surface rather than looking for a fully submerged stand. It spreads by runners, which lets you separate the young rosettes. Strong light is given for this entry. Do not automatically apply the growing habits of Limnobium laevigatum: the two species look alike, but differ in range and in tolerance of temperature.

Limnophila aquatica.presentation: Its finely cut, light green leaves give the stems a feathery look. This plant from India and Sri Lanka shows well in a group, where its branches make a bright bush. In an open-top tank, emersed shoots can bear small blue flowers.
Limnophila aquatica.culture: Good light encourages branching and more horizontal shoots. CO₂ and nutrients available in the water or substrate improve its growth. Leave room around the group, then take tip cuttings to fill out the planting. Its fine foliage contrasts well with broad-leaved plants.

Limnophila aromatica.origine: South Asia, Southeast Asia, East Asia, Australia
Limnophila aromatica.presentation: This Asian plant owes its name to the aromatic smell of its crushed leaves. Depending on the cultivated form, the submerged foliage may stay green or show red hues. In the trade it is often confused with Limnophila hippuridoides, whose leaf whorls are usually fuller.
Limnophila aromatica.culture: It needs good light, CO₂ and balanced feeding. Cuttings let you renew the stems. Check the form you receive before expecting a deep red: plants sold as “aromatica” are not all the same. Emersed growing succeeds on damp, rich soil in humid air.

Limnophila brownii.presentation: This marshweed from northern Australia bears very finely divided leaves in whorls smaller than those of Limnophila aquatica. Good light can tint the tips bronze, while the stems are often reddish brown. It brings light foliage and remains uncommon in the trade.
Limnophila brownii.culture: Medium to strong light, CO₂ and a steady supply of nutrients encourage fast growth. Stem cuttings let you renew the group. It can also form horizontal, runner-like shoots from which new stems rise: leave a little room around the stand for this spread.

Limnophila sessiliflora.origine: South, Southeast and East Asia: edges of still water, banks of rivers and streams
Limnophila sessiliflora.presentation:
The most widely grown Limnophila, long sold as “Ambulia”. Its stems bear whorls of finely cut leaves that recall cabombas, but it needs much less light.

Introduced outside its native range, it has become an invasive plant that threatens natural habitats, for example in the United States: never release cuttings into the wild.
Limnophila sessiliflora.culture:
Hardy and adaptable. With enough light and added CO2 it stays compact and its tips turn slightly red; in dim light its stems stretch and become bare. A complete fertiliser with iron is needed.

Its very fast growth means frequent trimming: cut the top of the stems and replant the tips, which also propagates it. Once it reaches the surface it branches a lot and can grow out of the water; submerged it almost never flowers, but grown emersed it bears purple flowers. Plant in a group, in the background.

Littorella uniflora.presentation: This small plant of European lake shores spreads by runners. In the wild it mostly grows on sandy bottoms in clear water that is poor in nutrients and lime. Its very slow underwater growth gives a planting that stays discreet for a long time, far from the ground covers that close the foreground in a few weeks.
Littorella uniflora.culture: Provide enough light and plenty of patience while the plants spread. The young plants from the runners fill in the gaps. Respect the parameters given for this entry without assuming that heavy feeding will necessarily speed it up: its natural habitat and slow pace call for a measured approach.

Lobelia cardinalis.origine: North America, Central America, tropical South America
Lobelia cardinalis.presentation: Underwater this Lobelia grows light green foliage and a habit easy to arrange in even stands. Its emersed form is different, with purple undersides and scarlet flowers. It has long been used in Dutch aquariums to build rows or “streets” of plants.
Lobelia cardinalis.culture: Medium light is enough, but more light gives a more compact habit. CO₂ and regular fertilisation improve vigour. Cut and replant the tops to control the height of the group. White roots may appear at the nodes: careful trimming helps keep a neat layout without expecting perfectly upright growth.

Ludwigia arcuata.presentation: Its narrow leaves and many branches make a fine stand with red and golden hues. This Ludwigia from the southeastern United States contrasts well with a dark background or small-leaved green plants. It looks very much like Ludwigia brevipes, sometimes sold under the same name.
Ludwigia arcuata.culture: Provide enough light and a steady supply of nutrients, especially trace elements to support the colours. CO₂ is not essential to grow it. Replant the tops and side shoots to thicken the group. The submerged forms look so alike that the emersed flowers are useful to tell L. arcuata from L. brevipes.

Ludwigia brevipes.presentation: This narrow-leaved Ludwigia forms a fine bush whose tips can turn red or orange. It comes from wetlands of the southeastern United States and brings a light texture to a raised foreground or the middle of the tank. Its aquatic form is very close to Ludwigia arcuata.
Ludwigia brevipes.culture: Good light is the first key to success. Keep nutrients available, especially if CO₂ speeds up growth. Trimming brings new side shoots; replant the healthy parts to fill out the stand. Check its identity when buying: the two Ludwigia are often confused and are easier to tell apart when they flower out of water.

Ludwigia glandulosa.presentation: Its lance-shaped, purplish-red leaves line very straight stems that branch little underwater. This American plant provides a sharp colour accent rather than a loose bush. It is sometimes sold under the incorrect names “perennis” or “peruensis”.
Ludwigia glandulosa.culture: Provide very strong light and enough iron and trace elements. When light is short, the leaves turn green and then drop; even well lit, the bottom of the stems may become bare. To get branches, cut the main shoot. Its colouring does not require deliberately pushing the tank into a nitrate deficiency.

Ludwigia helminthorrhiza.presentation: This floating American plant grows long stems, sometimes reddish leaves and strange white, spongy roots. These spindle-shaped breathing organs make it easy to recognise. In good conditions, white flowers with a yellow centre appear above the water.
Ludwigia helminthorrhiza.culture: It needs a lot of light and a large free surface for its fast-branching stems. Anchoring it in a nutrient-rich substrate helps. It suits a large open-top tank or a paludarium better than a small gallery of submerged plants. Emersed growing is easier and favours flowering.

Mayaca fluviatilis.origine: North America, Central America, Caribbean, tropical South America
Mayaca fluviatilis.presentation: Its small, fine leaves give the stems the light look of a moss, although it is a stem plant. This Mayaca from warm regions of the Americas grows above as well as below water, notably on the banks of small dark streams. It brings a soft texture to a planted layout.
Mayaca fluviatilis.culture: It prefers soft, acidic water, while being able to adapt to harder water. Good light, CO₂ and balanced feeding support its growth. Tips turning very pale can reveal a lack of iron. Take cuttings of healthy shoots to rejuvenate the stand and keep the foliage even.

Mayaca sellowiana.presentation: The very tightly packed foliage of this Mayaca makes fine shoots, more compact than those of Mayaca fluviatilis. Its name was wrongly applied to Rotala sp. “Nanjenshan”, which explains some of the confusion. In the true Mayaca the leaves are alternate and close to the stem, instead of being arranged in whorls.
Mayaca sellowiana.culture: The profile describes it as demanding under strong light, propagated by cuttings. Detailed experience remains scarce in the source consulted. First check the plant's identity: advice given for a Rotala “Nanjenshan” does not necessarily describe the plant received under the Mayaca sellowiana label.

Micranthemum umbrosum.origine: North America, Central America, tropical South America, southern South America
Micranthemum umbrosum.presentation: This Micranthemum forms a light green stand with many side shoots. It comes from American ditches, ponds and small streams, where it can switch between emersed and submerged forms with the season. Regular trimming lets you build a dense bush in the middle of the tank.
Micranthemum umbrosum.culture: Give it strong light: if it runs short, the lower leaves drop and the stems become fragile. CO₂ improves growth and leaf size, but growing without injection is possible. It can be slow to settle after a change of conditions. Cut and replant the shoots to gradually thicken the group.

Microsorum pteropus.origine: South, Southeast and East Asia: rocks and wood in streams and waterfalls, damp forest floor
Microsorum pteropus.presentation:
A fern very common in tropical and subtropical Asia, where it clings to rocks and wood in streams and waterfalls: some populations always live underwater, others on the damp forest floor. Botanists now place it in the genus *Leptochilus*, but the trade keeps the name *Microsorum pteropus*.

The species is very variable: beside the classic broad-leaved form there are forms with narrow leaves (“Narrow”), leaves split into a trident (“Trident”) or frilled at the tip (“Windeløv”). The black dots under the leaves are sporangia, the fern's reproductive organs, not a disease.
Microsorum pteropus.culture:
One of the easiest plants, ideal for beginners: moderate light is enough, with no fertiliser or CO2, and a gentle current suits it. Like the anubias, it forms a rhizome that rots if buried: tie it to a root or a stone, where its roots take hold within a few months.

It almost propagates itself: young plants appear under the leaves and at their tips, more rarely on the roots, and come away easily. The rhizome can also be cut with a knife. It also grows out of water, in a paludarium, as long as its support stays damp.

Murdannia keisak.origine: South Asia, Southeast Asia, East Asia
Murdannia keisak.presentation: Despite its narrow leaves set in two rows, this Asian plant is not a grass. It grows in rice fields, ditches and damp banks, where its stems float near the surface before rising at their tips. It can also grow fully submerged in the aquarium.
Murdannia keisak.culture: Provide medium to strong light and room for fast growth. Cuttings let you renew the group of stems. The land form is creeping, while the shoots can stand up at the surface: watch their direction to choose the trimming height and keep the outline you want in the tank.

Myriophyllum aquaticum (\"Normalform\").presentation: The usual form of this Myriophyllum grows long stems with finely cut foliage. Emersed shoots bear water-repellent, blue-green leaves; under strong light the submerged foliage can take on orange-brown tones. Its look therefore changes clearly when the stems reach the surface.
Myriophyllum aquaticum (\"Normalform\").culture: Give room to this form, which grows tall and is propagated by cuttings. Medium to strong light is given. Trim with growth at the surface in mind rather than expecting a permanent small bush. Other trade forms, including “Green” or dwarf types, differ in habit and colour.

Najas guadalupensis.origine: North America, Central America, Caribbean, tropical South America
Najas guadalupensis.presentation: Known as “Guppy grass”, this American plant quickly forms a network of submerged shoots. Undemanding, it is often used in breeding tanks. Its leaves look smooth at first glance but bear very small teeth. Its brittle stems explain how easily it spreads around the tank.
Najas guadalupensis.culture: It gets by with little equipment and propagates by fragments. Handle the stems gently; detached pieces can start growing elsewhere and make the planting harder to contain. Remove stray fragments if you want a tidy stand. It is often more useful in a breeding tank than in a highly structured layout.

Najas indica.origine: South Asia, Southeast Asia, East Asia
Najas indica.presentation: Its very narrow, toothed and curved leaves give the shoots a fine, decorative look. This aquatic plant from tropical and subtropical Asia has long been known in the hobby but remains uncommon in tanks. The botanical boundary between its name and Najas minor is debated in the sources.
Najas indica.culture: It is described as fairly undemanding, with medium to strong light given for this entry. Fragments are used to multiply the shoots. Keep the name of the plant you receive and check its origin rather than assuming that every Najas in the trade will share exactly the same habit or needs.

Nuphar japonica.presentation: This Japanese plant can produce submerged, floating or aerial leaves. It grows in still as well as running water and is cultivated as an ornamental aquatic plant. Several varieties exist, which explains differences in appearance between plants sold as Nuphar japonica.
Nuphar japonica.culture: Provide a setup where the foliage has room to develop, with good light for this entry. Dividing the rhizome is used to propagate it. Watch for floating leaves before deciding on its final place: the plant is not limited to a small bunch of leaves underwater.

Nymphaea gardneriana.origine: Caribbean, tropical South America, southern South America
Nymphaea gardneriana.presentation: The young submerged leaves of this American water lily can be orange-red, then turn green with age. The plant forms a small tuberous rhizome and spreads by runners. Some strains flower at night, but their behaviour in the aquarium differs with the origin of the batch.
Nymphaea gardneriana.culture: Strong light, warmth, a rich substrate and shallow water favour floating leaves. A strain introduced from Bolivia may lose its leaves and roots during several months of rest, while the “Santarem” form seems to grow more continuously. Keep the tuber if the foliage disappears, without promising the same cycle for every strain.

Nymphaea glandulifera.presentation: This water lily from Central America and northern South America forms a rosette from a tuberous organ. It can produce floating leaves and spread the planting by runners. This twin ability to grow underwater and towards the surface matters more when choosing its place than its botanical classification alone.
Nymphaea glandulifera.culture: Provide medium to strong light and water suited to the parameters of this entry. Separate the young plants produced by the runners to propagate it. Watch how much of the foliage reaches the surface so as to keep light for its neighbours. The detailed descriptions available remain limited; do not assume, without checking, that it follows another water lily's rest cycle.

Nymphoides aquatica.presentation: The thick storage roots clustered at its base recall a bunch of small bananas, hence the name “banana plant”. This Nymphoides comes from shallow, calm waters in the southeastern United States. Its storage organs set it apart from the other rosette plants in the catalogue.
Nymphoides aquatica.culture: The profile gives slow growth and strong light. Give it time to settle and grow new organs rather than comparing its pace with that of a fast stem plant. Propagation by plantlets is mentioned. The advice available remains limited in the detailed description consulted.

Nymphoides ezannoi.presentation: This African Nymphoides bears round floating leaves and white flowers with a yellow centre. Young plants may appear near the base of the leaves. In the aquarium their first submerged leaves soon give way to mostly floating growth, which suits an open-top tank well.
Nymphoides ezannoi.culture: Plant it in a nutrient-rich substrate: left simply floating without an anchor, it wastes away. Allow room at the surface and do not choose it to keep only small submerged foliage. The plantlets let you propagate it. A paludarium with an open water area can also show off its flowering.

Nymphoides indica.origine: Africa, Madagascar region, South Asia, Southeast Asia, East Asia, Australia, Oceania, North America, Central America, Caribbean, tropical South America
Nymphoides indica.presentation: Its round leaves float on the surface, often with a reddish or purplish underside. The pale flowers with a yellow centre have hairy fringes, giving the flowering a delicate look. This aquatic plant of warm regions grows in still or gently flowing water.
Nymphoides indica.culture: Leave free surface for the leaves rather than choosing it for a fully submerged stand. Runners and young plantlets let you propagate it. Medium to strong light is given for this entry. Thin the planting if the cover becomes too heavy for the other plants in the tank.

Ottelia alismoides.origine: Africa, South Asia, Southeast Asia, East Asia, Australia
Ottelia alismoides.presentation: This large aquatic plant grows as a rosette. It naturally lives in calm or flowing waters in tropical regions of Asia, Africa and Australia. Its size and habit make it an entry for a spot where a large plant can stay in view.
Ottelia alismoides.culture: It is rated difficult and needs strong light. Allow room for the rosette and follow the parameters of this profile rather than those of a small foreground plant. Propagation by seed is given. The source description gives no detailed method that would allow germination or growth to be promised within a set time.

Ottelia ulvifolia.origine: West Africa, Central Africa, East Africa, southern Africa, Madagascar region
Ottelia ulvifolia.presentation: Its large, slightly translucent leaves are wavy, sometimes twisted, and recall the sea lettuce that inspired its name. The form known in aquariums often bears reddish-brown marbling or small lines on a light green background. This plant from Africa and Madagascar makes a focal point in a tall aquarium.
Ottelia ulvifolia.culture: Allow plenty of room around the rosette, with strong light suited to its difficult growing. The leaves can grow large and do not suit a tight stand in a small tank. Propagation by seed is given. The different forms of the species do not all show exactly the same pattern.

Penthorum sedoides.presentation: Underwater this North American plant forms smaller, more compact shoots than its land form. Its light green, lance-shaped, toothed leaves give the stand a crisp texture. In natural wetlands it grows flower stalks and can take on pink or red autumn colours.
Penthorum sedoides.culture: It can be grown submerged, but is less documented than classic stem plants. Provide strong light and follow how the new shoots develop. Division and cuttings let you propagate it. A plant sold for a pond edge will look different from how it grows underwater.

Persicaria hydropiperoides.presentation: This American knotweed grows very upright and keeps fairly short internodes. Its subdued green can set off neighbouring red plants. In good conditions the leaves become very wavy. A dense group in the midground or background has more impact than a single stem.
Persicaria hydropiperoides.culture: It can survive in low light but becomes more attractive with strong light and good feeding. Provide an aquarium spacious enough for the group of stems. Cuttings are used to fill out the planting. Its habit stays upright: do not expect a creeping plant even when it gets a lot of light.

Persicaria praetermissa.origine: South Asia, Southeast Asia, East Asia, Australia
Persicaria praetermissa.presentation: This knotweed is also sold as “Ruby” or “Rubra”. Its narrow, lance-shaped leaves can show reddish-brown tones and a wine-coloured underside. The shoots tend to lean or grow horizontally, giving a less upright stand than some other Persicaria.
Persicaria praetermissa.culture: Plant it in the middle or back of the tank with enough light, then follow the fast spread of the shoots. Cuttings let you renew the group. The trade descriptions of these strains should not be extended without nuance to every population of the species: keep the name and origin of the batch you receive.

Phyllanthus fluitans.presentation: The round, water-repellent leaves float above small tufts of red roots. This plant from tropical America may recall a Salvinia, but bears only one leaf per node. The stronger the light, the more the foliage can take on reddish-brown tones. Tiny white flowers sometimes appear.
Phyllanthus fluitans.culture: Keep nutrients available to support its growth. The colour varies with the lighting: a green batch is not necessarily another plant. The fragile stems easily break into fragments that let you propagate it. It can also be grown emersed on a very damp, rich substrate.

Physostegia purpurea.presentation: Underwater this marsh plant from the southeastern United States forms a small rosette of long-stalked, elongated leaves. Its emersed form is much taller and can bear spikes of reddish-purple flowers. The difference between the two forms therefore matters when you receive a land-grown plant.
Physostegia purpurea.culture: It can be grown underwater but rarely is. Medium to strong light is given for this slow-growing entry. Division and separating young plants are used to propagate it. Do not expect, in a submerged aquarium, the tall flowering outline seen on a bank: the aquatic foliage stays more compact.

Pistia stratiotes.origine: Africa, Madagascar region, Central Asia, South Asia, Southeast Asia, East Asia, Australia, Oceania, Central America, Caribbean, tropical South America
Pistia stratiotes.presentation: The velvety leaves gather into floating rosettes, hence the name “water lettuce”. Many fine, feathery roots hang beneath the plant. This floater of warm regions lives in calm fresh water; its small flowers stay discreet, hidden near the base of the leaves.
Pistia stratiotes.culture: Leave the rosettes at the surface in a well-lit spot. Runners produce young plants used for propagation. The plant can form large colonies: remove the surplus to keep part of the surface free and avoid heavy shading of the bottom. In shallow water its roots can reach the substrate.

Pogostemon deccanensis.presentation: Very upright stems and fine foliage give the group a graphic look, close to needle-like vegetation. The source description tells how it spread from India under the names Pogostemon erectus and, before that, Rotala verticillaris. Emersed plants bear spikes of purple flowers, unlike those of Rotala.
Pogostemon deccanensis.culture: Provide medium to strong light and a place in the midground or background for the upright shoots. Cuttings let you renew the group. Keep track of the name you bought it under: its trade history and changes of name explain why older profiles do not always use the name found in this catalogue.

Pogostemon helferi.presentation: Nicknamed “little star” in Thai, this plant makes a very recognisable low accent. It grows naturally between the rocks of Thai streams, submerged for part of the year and then emersed when the level drops. It suits the foreground of a large tank or the middle of a small aquarium.
Pogostemon helferi.culture: Good light, CO₂ and enough nutrients encourage vigorous green foliage. Handle the plants gently: they bruise easily. Cut cleanly below a node to prepare a cutting. It can be tied to a stone or a root with a loose thread, without squeezing the tissue.

Potamogeton dentatus.presentation: This Japanese pondweed bears elongated leaves where the network of veins stays visible. The stems branch towards their upper part and can produce flower spikes at the surface. A truly submerged plant, it also grows rhizomes, which let it spread the group beyond the shoots already visible.
Potamogeton dentatus.culture: Give it a place in the midground or background with medium to strong light. Cuttings and young shoots from the runners let you multiply the planting. Watch this underground spread as well as the height of the stems. Detailed growing reports remain limited: avoid confusing this entry with the more common pondweeds.

Potamogeton gayi.presentation: This pondweed from southern South America grows fine rhizomes in the substrate, from which rise stems with long, narrow leaves. Supple and translucent, they range from green to orange-brown depending on the light. The shoots can grow tall, giving light but voluminous background vegetation.
Potamogeton gayi.culture: Allow room for this hardy, fast-growing plant. Medium to strong light is given. Separating offshoots and cuttings let you renew the planting. Its growth is not limited to the visible stems: the branching rhizomes can spread the group through the substrate.

Potamogeton perfoliatus.origine: Africa, Europe, Asia, Australia, the Americas
Potamogeton perfoliatus.presentation: This large pondweed lives in calm or slow-flowing, nutrient-rich water. It naturally forms belts of vegetation in lowland lakes and is found in many regions of the world. Its size makes it more of a plant for a spacious background than for a small stand.
Potamogeton perfoliatus.culture: The profile gives easy growing, fast growth and medium to strong light. Leave room for the shoots to develop and multiply the planting by cuttings. The detailed advice in the description consulted remains limited: follow the parameters of this entry rather than those of a smaller pondweed.

Proserpinaca palustris.origine: North America, Central America, Caribbean, southern South America
Proserpinaca palustris.presentation: Its foliage changes clearly when it moves to life underwater: the green emersed form gives way to more finely cut leaves, often orange-red. Several American forms exist, including a Cuban strain circulated in the hobby. It makes a colour accent without the speed of some red stem plants.
Proserpinaca palustris.culture: It takes time to acclimatise. Medium to strong light, CO₂ and balanced feeding bring out the colours; in particular keep up the iron supply. It forms few side shoots. After trimming, replant the top part to keep a presentable plant, possibly keeping the base to get new cuttings.

Ranunculus inundatus.presentation: Leaves divided into palmate lobes stand above creeping stems that advance over or in the substrate.
