This amphibious Australian buttercup makes a foreground with an unusual pattern, especially at the edge of a sandy area. Its yellow flowers appear on shoots grown out of water.
Ranunculus inundatus.culture: Strong light keeps the leaf stalks shorter; in the shade the leaves rise on long stalks. CO₂ and available nutrients support growth. It may be slow to take, then the branches spread quickly. Thin out a planting that is too crowded to keep the distinct leaf shape and avoid a messy carpet.

Riccia fluitans.presentation: This small floating plant forms a light green network that can also be held on the decor to make a submerged cushion. It became famous in aquascaping for its bright carpets, although not all strains are equally suited to growing underwater. Floating, it gives cover to young fish.
Riccia fluitans.culture: At the surface its needs for light and CO₂ remain modest. Submerged on a stone or wood, it needs more light, CO₂ and nutrients. Hold it in place with a net or thread, then trim the thick parts so the shaded base does not die. Fragments let you renew the cushions.

Rorippa aquatica.presentation: This American plant can form a small rosette or upright shoots, with leaves that are sometimes entire and toothed, sometimes deeply cut. Its look depends on the growing conditions. It stays fairly low underwater and offers the foreground foliage different from that of lawn-forming plants.
Rorippa aquatica.culture: Moderately cool water, medium to strong light and a nutrient-rich substrate suit it. Growth is very slow, even in good conditions. Young plants can form on detached leaves left floating, which lets you propagate it. Do not confuse this method with the quick rooting of a classic stem cutting.

Rotala indica.origine: South Asia, Southeast Asia, East Asia
Rotala indica.presentation: The true Rotala indica forms thick, very upright stems with small round to spoon-shaped leaves. It has also been circulated as Ammannia sp. “Bonsai”. The shoots branch little and can turn red at the tips. It is clearly different from Rotala rotundifolia, long sold under the same name.
Rotala indica.culture: Its rather slow growth needs good light and available nutrients. Plant a group of stems of different heights to show off its almost columnar habit. Cuttings are used to renew the stand. Check the plant you receive before following advice for a fast, red “Rotala indica” that might be R. rotundifolia.

Rotala macrandra.presentation: Its intense red colours make it a focal point among green plants. This Rotala of Indian origin is more demanding than several other species of the genus. A few well-placed stems are enough to create a strong accent; a stand that dominates too much can draw attention away from the rest of the layout.
Rotala macrandra.culture: Space the stems so that light also reaches their lower parts. Avoid shade, which can make the base die back. CO₂ helps bring together good growing conditions, along with steady fertilisation. After trimming, replant the healthiest top portions to rejuvenate the group rather than always keeping bare plants.

Rotala rotundifolia.origine: South, Southeast and East Asia, up to 2,700 m: marshes, banks and rice fields; naturalised in the southern United States
Rotala rotundifolia.presentation:
A classic aquarium plant, introduced around 1960 under the wrong name *Rotala indica*, a confusion that still lingers. Its name means “round-leaved”, but only the creeping marsh form has round leaves: underwater it bears elongated, oval to linear leaves. Out of water it flowers in pink spikes at the top of the stems.

Several forms are in the trade (“Green”, “H'Ra”, “Colorata”...), and their colour depends a great deal on growing conditions, which makes them hard to identify.
Rotala rotundifolia.culture:
Undemanding for a rotala, it grows under medium light but only takes on its pink to reddish hues under strong light. The best colours come with low nitrates and enough phosphates, iron and trace elements.

It is very easy to propagate: simply replant the tops or the side shoots. Trimmed, it branches and becomes bushy; it then needs frequent trimming so that light reaches the bottom of the stems. It goes in the midground or background.

Sagittaria platyphylla.presentation: This broad-leaved arrowhead comes from wetlands of the eastern and southeastern United States, with records in Central America. It has long been grown in aquariums but remains less common than Sagittaria subulata. Its rosette habit brings a different structure from a group of thin stems.
Sagittaria platyphylla.culture: Provide medium to strong light and leave room for the rosettes. Runners let you separate young plants to extend the planting. The source description remains sparse: do not automatically give it the height or lawn-forming behaviour of a Sagittaria subulata sold under a similar name.

Sagittaria subulata.presentation: This arrowhead forms rosettes of ribbon-like leaves and spreads quickly by runners. It can make a carpet, but its height varies a lot: a dense planting can produce much longer leaves than a sparse group. Small white flowers sometimes appear on floating stalks.
Sagittaria subulata.culture: It accepts moderate light and fairly hard water, with or without CO₂. A rich substrate or good feeding in the water supports growth. Yellowing leaves can signal a lack of iron. Thin the runners if you want to keep a low planting; the label “pusilla” does not guarantee a permanently dwarf plant.

Samolus valerandi.origine: Europe, East Asia, North America, Central America, Caribbean, tropical South America
Samolus valerandi.presentation: This marsh plant forms a spreading rosette of light green leaves rounded at the tip, a little reminiscent of lamb's lettuce. It grows on damp soils and the edges of fresh or brackish water. Out of water, small white flowers can appear on a taller stalk.
Samolus valerandi.culture: Provide strong light for this difficult, slow-growing entry. Propagation by seed is mentioned in the profile. Give the rosette time to produce new leaves and follow how it adapts to submersion. The description available does not justify promising growing as easy as that of a common aquatic plant.

Saururus cernuus.presentation: Its large heart-shaped leaves contrast with fine-leaved plants. This American marsh plant grows straight underwater and can quickly pass the surface if allowed to rise. It was long used to build rows of plants in Dutch aquariums.
Saururus cernuus.culture: Strong light, CO₂ and regular feeding encourage large, vigorous leaves. The foliage renews slowly and can carry spot algae. Replant the tops after trimming; floating stem fragments can also produce young plants. The emersed form is much easier to grow, but its runners need to be contained.

Spiranthes odorata.presentation: This American marsh orchid can last underwater for a long time, which makes it unusual in an aquatic catalogue. Its fairly thick leaves contain air-filled tissue. Out of water it becomes more vigorous and produces flowers arranged in a spiral around upright stalks.
Spiranthes odorata.culture: Submerged, it grows very slowly and stays discreet. Emersed growing favours flowering. Young plants form on the spreading roots, which lets you propagate it. Check the name when buying: Spiranthes cernua is another, closely related species, and not all marsh orchids tolerate lasting submersion equally.

Stratiotes aloides.presentation: Its long, stiff leaves with spiny edges form a large rosette, giving it the look of a “water pineapple”. In the European and Asian habitats where it lives, it overwinters on the bottom and rises again when the water warms up. In summer some leaves stand above the surface and the long roots can reach the mud.
Stratiotes aloides.culture: Allow plenty of space for the rosette and its roots. Well known as a pond plant, it can also be grown in a tropical aquarium according to the source. Division and separating young plants are used to propagate it. Take its cycle and size into account rather than choosing it as a small, stable foreground rosette.

Taxiphyllum barbieri.origine: Southeast Asia; botanists have recorded it in the wild only in Vietnam
Taxiphyllum barbieri.presentation:
The most widely grown moss in aquariums. The name “Java moss” first referred to *Vesicularia dubyana*, grown in Europe for decades, before *Taxiphyllum barbieri*, introduced in 1969 as “Bogor moss” and more vigorous, replaced it almost everywhere. The bryologist Zennosuke Iwatsuki identified it as early as 1982; GBIF now places it in the genus *Ectropothecium*.

Its thin, much-branched stems cling to any support with rhizoids, small brown filaments that act as roots: wood, stone, and even plastic or glass covered in algae.
Taxiphyllum barbieri.culture:
Very undemanding in terms of light and water quality. Under strong light it grows denser and paler; in dim light, darker and looser. It tolerates 30 °C, but grows faster and looks better around 24 °C. An iron-rich fertiliser and added CO2 help without being necessary.

Tie it to a root or a stone with nylon thread until it takes hold, then trim it with scissors to keep the shape you want. Dense and bushy, it gives shelter to fry and shrimp, and a place to spawn.

Tonina fluviatilis.presentation: The shoots stay very straight and bear fresh green foliage with an unusual pattern. This plant of slow blackwater streams in tropical America makes a crisp accent in the midground or background. Its moderate growth allows structured layouts, but its needs reserve it for tanks prepared for demanding plants.
Tonina fluviatilis.culture: Provide soft water, an acidic substrate, strong light and CO₂. Keep nutrients available, especially iron and trace elements. Do not let faster neighbours smother it. To propagate it, use short tops or side shoots: long cuttings readily grow visible roots on their lower parts.

Utricularia aurea.origine: South Asia, Southeast Asia, East Asia, Australia
Utricularia aurea.presentation: This large, rootless bladderwort forms shoots with very finely cut leaves. Yellowish green in the aquarium, it can be redder in the wild. It floats below the surface of tropical waters in Asia and Australia; its yellow flowers rise on stalks. Its small traps remain poorly developed, or even absent, in the aquarium.
Utricularia aurea.culture: Let it float or hold the tips in the substrate like upright stems. Undemanding, it accepts soft to harder water and grows fast. Fragments let you propagate it. Set aside enough room and thin the cover so it does not hide the other plants.

Utricularia gibba.origine: Africa, Madagascar region, Europe, Asia, Australia, Oceania, the Americas
Utricularia gibba.presentation: Its extremely thin stems tangle into cushions in the water or between other plants. Small traps catch microscopic organisms, with no danger to fry or young shrimp observed in the source. It can, however, invade mosses and plant carpets, often after being introduced by accident.
Utricularia gibba.culture: It tolerates many conditions and regrows from tiny fragments. To contain it, patiently remove the shoots with tweezers and check for pieces left in the stands. Well-tuned fertilisation is not enough to stop it spreading. It mostly interests carnivorous plant enthusiasts, rather than a layout where every stand must stay separate.

Utricularia graminifolia.presentation: Small, linear, light green leaves make a carpet reminiscent of a lawn. This Asian bladderwort anchors itself with root-like organs and bears tiny carnivorous traps. Unlike many floating bladderworts, it forms a true ground cover; emersed growing can give pale purple flowers.
Utricularia graminifolia.culture: Provide medium to strong light and follow carefully how it takes, as it is rated difficult. Fragments let you extend the planting. There is no need to feed it with animals: the source says it can live without this extra resource and reports no danger observed for young fish or shrimp.

Vallisneria spiralis.origine: Africa, West Asia and warm regions of Europe (Italy...): calm or flowing water
Vallisneria spiralis.presentation:
A “classic” plant, grown since the early days of fishkeeping. Its name does not come from its leaves, which are straight and ribbon-like, but from the stalk of the female flower, which coils into a spiral after flowering and pulls the fruit down to the bottom.

Under this name the trade sells plants of very different sizes, most often with smooth, fairly narrow leaves. “V. spiralis” imported from Malaysia turned out to be *Vallisneria denseserrulata*, an Asian species that is almost impossible to tell apart without its flowers.
Vallisneria spiralis.culture:
Very easy, it grows under almost any light and in almost any water, from 5 to 30 °C. It does not live out of water. It is planted in the background, where its long leaves form a curtain: 30 to 50 cm in Tropica's striped “Tiger” form.

It spreads by itself through runners, and the young plants that appear around the mother plant are enough to propagate it; simply pull out the surplus.
